Water Amendment Bill 2018 - Third Reading - Pass the bill

The Water Amendment Bill 2018 was moved to restore the disallowed Northern Basin Review amendment to the Murray-Darling Basin Plan, granting the minister a limited directions power to have the authority remake the instrument, aiming to provide certainty for basin states and communities to meet the 30 June 2019 deadline for sustainable diversion limit compliant water resource plans.

The speaker argued that the Turnbull government's incompetence and indifference forced the Water Amendment Bill 2018, citing failures like refusing a judicial inquiry into alleged water theft and mismanagement of water buybacks. Labor supports the bill but insists on full implementation of the 2012 Murray-Darling Basin Plan, including the additional 450 gigalitres for South Australia, warning that any weakening threatens the basin's sustainability.

The speaker supported the Water Amendment Bill 2018, which implements a 70-gigalitre correction in the Northern Basin Review, returning water from environmental use to productive agriculture. He argued for applying a social and economic test to the remaining 450 gigalitres of "up water," citing significant job losses in irrigation regions like Mildura (38%), Merbein (50%), and Swan Hill (53%), and criticised Labor and the Greens for ignoring community impacts.

The opposition will support the Water Amendment Bill 2018, allowing the government to reissue a previously disallowed instrument after successful negotiations. Labor will facilitate the bill's passage without amendment, acknowledging the Murray-Darling Basin Plan requires compromise and is not an ideal solution for any party.

The Water Amendment Bill 2018 is needed to get the Murray-Darling Basin Plan back on track, with the speaker criticising political interference—particularly from South Australia—and praising a compromise that includes Indigenous water allocations and compliance measures. The speaker also defended irrigators and the cotton industry against allegations from the Four Corners program, stating that water reforms have taken decades and that communities want the process finalised.

The speaker argued that the Water Amendment Bill 2018 is needed to lock in an additional 450 gigalitres of environmental water for the River Murray, building on the existing 2,750 gigalitre recovery and $1.77 billion funding package from 2012, and to protect the river from future droughts and water theft.

The speaker supported the Water Amendment Bill 2018 and the agreement to deliver the Murray-Darling Basin Plan in full, noting the SDL adjustment mechanism reduces water recovery by 605 gigalitres, but expressed concern about the additional 450 gigalitres of environmental water and the 80,000 megalitre daily flow target at the South Australian border, citing socio-economic losses including $120 million at the farm gate, 678 job losses, and population declines of up to 45.6% in communities like Wakool.

The speaker argued that the Murray-Darling Basin Plan has driven progress through community engagement, innovation, and bipartisan cooperation, noting that cotton growers in the southern basin have reduced water usage by 40%. They stressed the need for transparency, compliance, and fair water markets, while acknowledging ongoing challenges for dairy farmers and the importance of funding for First Nations water entitlements and the 450-gigalitre environmental target.

The speaker argued that the Water Amendment Bill 2018 is crucial for restoring the Murray-Darling Basin Plan, which was "hanging by a thread," and highlighted the need for bipartisan support to address overextraction, climate change pressures, and declining streamflow. They criticised Prime Minister Turnbull's decision to place the plan under the agriculture ministry, supported the return of 3,200 gigalitres of water (including an additional 450 gigalitres), and endorsed new measures for compliance, scrutiny of sustainable diversion limit adjustment projects, and Indigenous cultural water outcomes.

Federal Labor will fight for a healthy Murray River, criticising the National Party and the member for New England over water theft and corruption, and supports the delivery of 450 gigalitres of environmental flows and 605 gigalitre projects under the Water Amendment Bill 2018.

Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018 - Adoption of Report - Don't insist on amendments

The Liberal-National coalition argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018 delivers lower, fairer, and simpler taxes, providing tax relief to low- and middle-income earners first, protecting against bracket creep, and ensuring 94% of taxpayers pay no more than 32.5 cents in tax by 2024-25. The speaker claimed Labor supports over $200 billion in higher taxes, including on housing, savings, family businesses, and retirees, while the coalition’s seven-year plan is affordable and fiscally responsible.

The government's tax plan offers only modest relief that does not compensate for cuts to penalty rates, health insurance, energy, pensions, and public services; the bill should be split to pass the 1 July 2018 tax cuts for low- and middle-income earners immediately, while opposing the later stages.

The speaker argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018 delivers responsible, affordable tax relief in three steps, with 94% of taxpayers projected to face a marginal rate of 32.5% or less by 2024-25, and highlighted that 4.4 million Australians will receive $530 in immediate relief in 2018-19. The speaker also noted the government has created 415,000 jobs in 2017, reduced welfare dependency to 15%, and legislated over $41 billion in budget repair measures.

The speaker argued that tax cuts improve equality and fairness, citing the US under Reagan and Clinton and the UK under Thatcher and Blair, and claimed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018 is critical for reducing inequality in Australia. They contrasted this with high taxes and government interference in Venezuela under Hugo Chavez, which they said caused a refugee crisis.
The government's tax plan was abandoned soon after introduction, with supporters relying on discredited trickle-down economics.

The speaker argued in support of the Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018, advocating for tax cuts so that hardworking Australians keep more of their income, and noted over one million jobs created since the government took office, alongside tax relief for low- and middle-income earners and repair of a $48 billion deficit inherited from Labor.

The speaker supported the Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018, arguing it delivers tax cuts for low- and middle-income earners, with a maximum benefit of $530 for those earning between $48,000 and $90,000, and a projected surplus in 2019-20. The speech also highlighted a $225 million investment in the Frankston to Baxter train line duplication and criticised Labor's tax policies.

The speech opposed the Treasury Laws Amendment (Personal Income Tax Plan) Bill 2018, arguing it relied on discredited trickle-down economics and an arbitrary 23.9% government size cap, with tax cuts disproportionately favouring high-income earners—citing a $7,225 benefit for a $200,000 earner versus $509 for the median Shortland worker. The alternative proposed was larger tax cuts for low- and middle-income earners, funded by closing tax loopholes, and rejecting cuts to services.

The speaker moved the second reading of the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 and introduced the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme Bill, which establishes registration obligations for persons or entities with arrangements or activities on behalf of foreign principals to provide transparency about foreign influence in Australia.

The speaker argued that the two national security bills were initially flawed with overreach, threatening journalists, charities, academics, and civil liberties, but after extensive bipartisan committee work and 60 recommendations, the amendments now properly target foreign interference while safeguarding freedoms. The speaker also criticised the government's rushed process and lack of consultation, noting the bills were significantly improved through the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security.

The speaker argued that the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 and related bill are necessary to protect Australia’s sovereignty and democratic institutions, asserting that the nation speaks with bipartisan unity against foreign threats. The speaker referenced Prime Minister John Curtin’s 1942 wartime address to emphasise Australia’s historical resolve, and noted that the Parliamentary Joint Committee on Intelligence and Security (PJCIS) has included reviews and safeguards in the legislation.

The speaker opposed the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 and the Foreign Influence Transparency Scheme Bill 2017, arguing their definitions of 'national security' and 'foreign influence' are too broad and could criminalise protest, whistleblowing, and reporting to international bodies. He also criticised the government's hypocrisy, noting that 12 MPs had been flown to China by Huawei while claiming to be concerned about foreign influence, and warned that Australia is becoming a "pre police state" with over 60 security reforms since 9/11.

The speaker argued that the National Security Legislation Amendment (Espionage and Foreign Interference) Bill 2017 criminalises dissent, broadens national security definitions, and could jail protesters against projects like the Adani coalmine, while criticising the rushed passage of 50 pages of amendments without proper scrutiny.
